By Jonathan Velez , Personal Finance Writer & Editor · Reviewed against primary sources · Updated November 10, 2026 Pick a robo-advisor if you want automated investing for one defined goal and accept little human contact. The SEC says robo-advisers often seek to offer lower costs, but a flat monthly fee can cost more than a percentage fee on a small balance. Pick a human adviser if you need advice beyond investing or want a person to talk to. This comparison rests on Investor.gov, two SEC investor bulletins and a 2019 SEC chairman statement. Both models can provide ongoing portfolio management, but their operational methods and service scopes differ. An automated digital investment advisory program collects your goals and risk tolerance through an online questionnaire, then builds and manages a portfolio. A human investment adviser provides ongoing investment advice and monitoring, and can deliver planning services alongside securities management. Robo-Advisor vs Human Financial Advisor: Side-by-Side Robo-Advisor Human Financial Advisor Primary service model Automated digital program creating and managing an investment portfolio Ongoing advice, portfolio monitoring, and optional broad financial planning Intake method Online questionnaire collecting financial goals, time horizon, and risk tolerance Conversation with a person to gather your needs Typical fee structures Asset-based percentage fees or monthly subscriptions such as $3, $5, or $10 Ongoing asset-based fee on total portfolio value or negotiated planning fees Human contact Ranges from technical support only to hybrid access or minimum balance thresholds Direct personal conversations with an investment professional Standard of conduct Fiduciary duty of care and loyalty Fiduciary duty for investment advisers. Brokers follow Regulation Best Interest Key regulatory disclosures Form ADV Part 1, Part 2A brochure, and Form CRS relationship summary Form ADV Part 1, Part 2A brochure, Part 2B supplements, and Form CRS Underlying investments Many use ETFs. Some limit products to broad-based ETFs Securities the adviser recommends (Investor.gov) 📣 Building in finance? Put your product in front of readers comparing options on this page. Advertise With Us → Which should you choose? A robo-advisor fits a reader who wants automated investing for a defined goal and accepts little human contact, and the cost depends on your balance. A human adviser fits a reader who needs advice beyond investing or wants a person to call. If the human is a registered investment adviser, the duty of care and loyalty is the same as a robo-advisor's. If the person is a broker or dual registrant, a different standard may apply, shown in Form CRS. This outcome changes if an automated platform provides a hybrid human adviser at your balance level, or if the human is broker-only. Read both firms' relationship summaries and Form ADV Part 2 disclosures to compare all-in costs and human access before opening an account. Robo-Advisor or Financial Advisor: Which Fits Your Situation Your choice between a robo-advisor and a traditional human advisor depends on the complexity of your financial profile and your preferences for personal support. If your goal is automated investing for a defined goal, an automated platform builds and manages a portfolio. According to the SEC Investor Bulletin on Robo-Advisers published by the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) Office of Investor Education and Advocacy (OIEA), a robo-advisor is an automated digital investment advisory program. These platforms collect your financial goals, investment time horizon, household income, other assets, and risk tolerance through an online questionnaire. The software then uses that collected information to build and manage an investment portfolio for you. Robo-advisors often seek to offer lower costs and fees, and some require lower account minimums. Human investment advisers operate differently during the initial evaluation process. As detailed by Investor.gov on Investment Advisers , an investment adviser is a firm or person that provides investment advice about securities for compensation. These professionals typically provide ongoing advice about buying, selling, or holding investments, monitor performance, and may give planning services. Unlike an automated program that relies on an online questionnaire, a traditional adviser can hold a conversation to gather your needs. What Robo-Advisors and Financial Advisors Cost You Comparing costs between automated platforms and personal advisers requires examining both fee structures and auxiliary account expenses. Most traditional investment advisers charge an asset-based fee calculated as a percentage of the total assets held in your account. As noted in the Investor.gov Relationship Summary (Form CRS) guidance, advisers are generally focused on your portfolio over time and typically paid an ongoing asset-based fee on total account value. Robo-advisors use diverse pricing frameworks, ranging from asset-based percentage fees to recurring subscriptions. The SEC Investor Bulletin on Subscription-Based Advisory Fees notes that subscription pricing entails a set recurring fee, typically billed monthly. For smaller robo-adviser accounts, that fee might be $3, $5, or $10 per month for investment management. The SEC bulletin warns that on small balances a flat monthly fee can cost more than a traditional asset-based fee. A $3 monthly fee on a $500 account is $36 a year, more than 7 percent. Advisory management charges do not encompass all investment expenses. Both human advisers and robo-advisers invest client money into underlying funds that carry internal operational expenses. The SEC bulletin on robo-advisers notes that many digital programs build portfolios using exchange-traded funds (ETFs), which deduct ongoing management expenses from fund performance. Similarly, clients may pay other fees such as brokerage, custody, and fund expenses. For detailed comparisons of conventional percentage models and fixed advisory retainers, read our comparison of flat-fee vs AUM advisors , or explore specific automated choices in our guide to the best robo-advisors . How Much Human Contact You Get with Each Option The level of personal contact varies widely across advisory options and should dictate which path you select. When working with a traditional human financial advisor, direct personal dialogue serves as the foundation of the relationship. You talk directly with a person who gathers your needs and provides ongoing advice. Robo-advisory platforms deliver varying levels of human communication. The SEC bulletin on robo-advisers explains that some digital programs offer access to an investment professional, often described as a hybrid or bionic model. Other automated platforms restrict human contact entirely to technical support staff. Furthermore, some automated firms condition access to human professionals on maintaining a minimum account size, leaving smaller account holders with purely digital interfaces. Unlike traditional advisory relationships, digital programs typically lack an initial conversation with a person to assess your personal needs. The SEC bulletin points out that robo-adviser recommendations are limited by the information requested, and the burden to update your profile data falls squarely on you. If your information changes, the robo-advisor cannot incorporate those developments until you update your profile. Duty of Care Depends on How Your Advisor Is Registered The legal standard of conduct governing your investment professional depends entirely on their regulatory registration. In a July 2019 statement , then SEC Chairman Jay Clayton explained that the investment adviser fiduciary duty is comprised of a duty of care and a duty of loyalty. This fiduciary framework applies to registered investment advisers, requiring them to act in the best interest of their clients and avoid placing their own financial interests ahead of the client's interests. Robo-advisors registered with the SEC operate as registered investment advisers, which means they owe clients an adviser fiduciary duty of care and loyalty. Similarly, human professionals who operate as registered investment advisers are held to this same fiduciary standard. However, many individual financial professionals do not operate solely as investment advisers. Some professionals are registered representatives of broker-dealers, while others are dual registrants licensed as both brokers and investment advisers. For broker-dealers, Regulation Best Interest establishes the governing standard of conduct, requiring brokers to act in the best interest of retail customers when making investment recommendations. Determining which standard applies to your advisory relationship requires reviewing regulatory disclosure documents. According to the SEC Investor Bulletin on Form ADV , retail investors should review Form ADV Part 2 and the Form CRS relationship summary. Form ADV Part 2A serves as an adviser's primary narrative brochure, detailing advisory business practices, fee schedules, conflict points, and disciplinary history across 18 standardized items. Form CRS explicitly states whether a firm is an investment adviser, a broker-dealer, or a dual registrant. You can verify firm registrations and review public filings on the SEC Investment Adviser Public Disclosure (IAPD) database. Who Each Option Is Not For and What Would Change the Answer A robo-advisor may not fit you if you want a person to call or your finances include accounts its questionnaire does not ask about. The SEC bulletin says some robo-advisers offer hybrid access to an investment professional and some use tax loss harvesting, so ask each one. A human adviser may not fit a small balance with one simple goal. See is a financial advisor worth it for the break-even math. Specific operational changes can flip this general advisory recommendation. If an automated robo-advisory platform offers a hybrid service tier with an investment professional at your balance, the robo-advisor may satisfy your need for personal communication. If you want to understand automated services in depth, read our overview of what a robo-advisor is . Conversely, if a human professional you interview is registered exclusively as a broker-dealer representative rather than an investment adviser, the regulatory baseline shifts. Checking Form CRS confirms whether your prospective advisor operates as an investment adviser or a broker. Reviewing your personal planning targets with our retirement calculator will help clarify which advisory model supports your goals. Frequently asked questions Are robo-advisors better than financial advisors? Robo-advisors are better for investors who want automated investment management for a defined goal and who do not require personal financial planning. The right option depends on your account size and the breadth of services you require. Is a robo-advisor a good idea? A robo-advisor is a good idea if you want an automated portfolio built with exchange-traded funds. The SEC says robo-advisers often seek to offer lower costs, though dollar fees can add up on a small balance. It may not fit if you want a dedicated person to call, but some robo-advisors offer hybrid professional access or tax loss harvesting, so check each service. Robo-advisor vs financial planner: what is the difference? A robo-advisor is an automated digital investment advisory program that builds a portfolio from your questionnaire answers. Financial planner is a job title, and Investor.gov lists a financial planner among the people you can hire to help with investment decisions, so ask what services and registration the person has. See financial advisor vs financial planner . When Should You Switch Financial Advisors? By Jonathan Velez , Personal Finance Writer & Editor · Reviewed against primary sources · Updated November 10, 2026 You should switch financial advisors when your current adviser's services, all-in costs, or conflicts of interest no longer fit what you need. Move in this order: read your contract's termination terms, check the new adviser on IAPD, open the account at the receiving firm, and let that firm start the transfer so you do not sell holdings or take a check yourself. Tools for this journey Investing → Retirement → Net worth → The Steps to Switch Financial Advisors in Order The right moment to switch financial advisors is when your adviser's fee structure, scope of services, or disclosed conflicts no longer serve your financial goals. Our suggested order: Review your current advisory agreement for termination terms and fee terms. Research prospective replacements on official public registries. Open your new account at the receiving firm. Submit a Transfer Initiation Form to your receiving firm so they pull the assets directly. Pause all buying and selling while the automated transfer runs. Confirm delivery of your holdings. Step Who acts What to check Source 1. Review contract Client Termination terms and fee schedule Investor.gov advisory guidance 2. Check credentials Client Form ADV Part 2 brochure and disciplinary history SEC Form ADV bulletin 3. Open new account Client and receiving firm Ask the receiving firm about policies or constraints that could affect the transfer FINRA transfer rules 4. Start transfer Receiving firm Transfer Initiation Form and eligible assets FINRA transfer rules 5. Freeze trading Client and both firms Whether either firm freezes trading during the transfer FINRA transfer rules 6. Confirm completion Both firms and client How each firm tells you the transfer is complete FINRA transfer rules Checks That Show the Advice or Fees No Longer Fit According to Investor.gov , an investment adviser is a firm or person that provides investment advice about securities for compensation. Investor.gov states that investment advisers are required to act in your best interest and not put their interest ahead of yours. Even so, the way advisers make money creates conflicts of interest to ask about (Investor.gov). Evaluate five baseline questions to determine whether your professional relationship still works: Services you need: Does your current adviser provide ongoing advice about buying, selling, or holding investments alongside broader financial planning, or has your situation outgrown their service limits? Cost and fee models: Are you paying an ongoing fee based on the total value of all assets in your account when your transaction volume or service needs have dropped? How the adviser is paid: As outlined in Investor.gov's guide to Form CRS , brokers are generally transactional and paid through commissions or markups per trade, while advisers typically charge an asset-based fee. From a cost perspective, you may prefer an asset-based fee if you want ongoing advice or want someone to make investment decisions for you. Disclosed conflicts: Does the way the adviser makes money create conflicts of interest to ask about? Our guide on financial advisor conflicts of interest outlines how these arrangements operate. Disciplinary record: Has the individual or firm accumulated legal or disciplinary history? If your adviser cannot clearly justify their fees or resolve disclosed conflicts, switching to another professional is a reasonable step. What to Read in Your Advisory Contract Before You Leave Before contacting a new firm, locate and read your original investment advisory agreement. Investor.gov notes that the exact services and fees you receive depend on the contract you negotiate. The contract governs the formal terms of your relationship, including termination procedures and fee terms. While your contract contains legal termination mechanics, your adviser's Form ADV Part 2A brochure details their broad billing practices. The SEC Form ADV bulletin states that Part 2A is a plain-English narrative brochure containing 18 standardized items. The brochure covers fees and compensation, explaining how the firm is compensated, its fee schedule, whether fees are negotiable, whether fees are billed directly or deducted from client accounts, and other fees such as brokerage, custody, and fund expenses. Form ADV Part 2A does not contain your specific termination clause. You must examine your signed contract to identify any notice requirements. If you have questions about ending the agreement, ask your adviser in writing to confirm the steps required to terminate the contract. How to Check the New Adviser Selecting a replacement adviser requires independent verification before you sign an agreement or open accounts. Advisers generally must register with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) or state regulatory authorities. Investor.gov advises investors to check both the firm and the individual representative. You can research both the individual and the firm using the Investment Adviser Public Disclosure (IAPD) database, which is also accessible via the Check Out Your Investment Professional tool on Investor.gov. If the professional operates as a registered broker or dual registrant, you can review their background on FINRA BrokerCheck . When reviewing records on IAPD, examine three filings: Form ADV Part 1: A structured form detailing the firm's business, ownership structure, client types, employees, business affiliations, and disciplinary events involving the adviser or its staff. Form ADV Part 2A Brochure: The primary disclosure document covering 18 standard items, including advisory services, assets under management, fee schedules, methods of analysis, risk of loss, and a ten-year history of material disciplinary events. Our breakdown on how to read Form ADV explains each item. Form ADV Part 2B Brochure Supplement: A disclosure detailing the specific individuals who formulate investment advice, have direct client contact, or exercise discretionary authority. It lists their educational background, business experience over the past five years, disciplinary events, and other business activities. Reviewing Form ADV Part 3, also known as Form CRS, provides a summary of the firm's services, fees, conflicts, standard of conduct, and disciplinary history. You can use these disclosures to prepare relevant questions to ask a financial advisor during introductory meetings, or reference our guide on how to choose a financial advisor . How the Account Moves According to FINRA , most customer accounts move between broker-dealers through ACATS, and cash, stocks, bonds and listed options are readily transferable that way. To begin an account transfer, you complete a Transfer Initiation Form (TIF) and submit it directly to your receiving firm. Once submitted, validation and delivery between broker-dealers generally takes about three to four business days. Transfers originating from non-broker-dealers, such as banks, credit unions, or mutual fund companies, generally take more time. Furthermore, accounts that require a third-party custodian, like an individual retirement account (IRA), may require additional processing time. A receiving firm is not legally required to accept your account. The most common reason a firm rejects a transfer involves credit policies, but rejections also happen when an account holds nontransferable assets. Nontransferable assets include proprietary products exclusive to the delivering firm or third-party mutual funds that lack a selling agreement with the new institution. FINRA rules require firms to notify customers of any nontransferable assets and provide alternatives. While the transfer is actively processing, avoid buying or selling securities. FINRA warns that buying and selling during an active transfer often complicates and delays the process, and some firms freeze all trading in the account until the transfer completes. Retirement Money: Direct Transfer vs a Check to You Moving retirement assets requires careful attention to tax administration rules. According to the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) , most pre-retirement payments from a retirement plan or an IRA can be rolled over by depositing the funds into another eligible plan or IRA within 60 days. You can also arrange for your financial institution or retirement plan to directly transfer the payment to another plan or IRA. The IRS states that the one-per-year rollover limit does not apply to rollovers from traditional IRAs to Roth IRAs (conversions), trustee-to-trustee transfers to another IRA, IRA-to-plan rollovers, plan-to-IRA rollovers, or plan-to-plan rollovers. Under IRS rules, if taxes are withheld on a distribution paid to you and you roll the money over within the 60-day window, you must use other funds to make up the withheld amount. Because the tax effects of selling investments in taxable accounts or distributing retirement funds depend on individual circumstances, consult a qualified tax professional before initiating any liquidation. Our Takeaway on When to Switch Financial Advisors In our editorial judgment, the decision to switch financial advisors should be driven by measurable gaps in service, misaligned costs, or unaddressed conflicts of interest. Review your advisory contract for termination rules, verify your new professional on IAPD or FINRA BrokerCheck, open your new account, and let the receiving institution initiate the transfer via ACATS. This process applies to retail clients working with SEC-registered or state-registered investment advisers and broker-dealers across the United States. Your next concrete step is to locate your current contract and read its termination clause before asking your new firm for a Transfer Initiation Form. Who This Is Not For and What Would Change the Answer This transition guide is not intended for investors seeking to switch financial advisors simply due to normal, short-term market declines. A short-term market move is not by itself a check that shows the advice or fees no longer fit. Certain contractual or portfolio conditions can change the decision to switch: Termination charges: If your current advisory contract contains termination charges, that cost can change the answer. Proprietary, nontransferable holdings: If your portfolio holds proprietary funds, the receiving firm is not required to accept those nontransferable assets. Pending retirement plan events: A pending tax event can change the timing of your switch. Asking both firms about your holdings and contract terms beforehand shows you costs and trading freezes before they surprise you. Frequently asked questions Can you switch financial advisors? Yes, you can switch financial advisors. Your ability to terminate the relationship and the required notice period depend on the specific terms negotiated in your written advisory contract. Is it hard to switch financial advisors? It is a short procedure when your assets can move as they are. You complete a Transfer Initiation Form with the receiving firm, and most broker-dealer accounts then move through ACATS in about three to four business days. Accounts at banks, credit unions or fund companies, and IRAs, take longer, and the receiving firm can refuse nontransferable assets. Does it cost money to switch financial advisors? It can. Your advisory contract sets the fees and terms (Investor.gov), so read its termination terms and ask both the current and the receiving firm what they charge before you start. The sources we read list no standard switching fee. What happens when you switch financial advisors? When you switch, your receiving firm requests your assets from your old firm using a Transfer Initiation Form. Your positions move through an automated transfer service like ACATS, after which your new adviser takes over portfolio monitoring and management. The SEC investor bulletin on Form ADV calls the Part 2A brochure the primary disclosure document for investment advisers. Learning how to read Form ADV gives you a direct look at how an advisory firm operates and how its professionals get paid. The document serves as the uniform registration filing for both federal and state authorities. Reviewing the brochure, the individual supplement, and the relationship summary prepares you to spot material disciplinary events and ask direct questions during your first meeting. Tools for this journey Investing → Retirement → Net worth → How to Find and Read Form ADV in the Order That Helps To start your search, open the Investor.gov Check Out Your Investment Professional tool, which directs you straight to the SEC Investment Adviser Public Disclosure database . This public portal lets you search by individual name or firm name. The SEC does not set a reading order for clients. Our suggested order is an editorial judgment designed to help you absorb the most practical information first: Search for the advisory firm on the SEC public portal to confirm its registration status. Open the Form ADV Part 2A narrative brochure to review services, fee schedules, conflicts, and disciplinary history. Open the Form ADV Part 2B brochure supplement to review the specific background of the individual who manages your portfolio. Read the Form ADV Part 3 relationship summary to compare service tiers, conduct standards, and basic fee models across firms. Check the Form ADV Part 1 filing for formal corporate ownership, affiliate connections, and recorded disciplinary items. Taking this sequence lets you focus on fees and conflicts before reviewing corporate census data. Anything unclear during your reading should become an immediate question for the professional. What Each Part of Form ADV Contains According to the SEC investor bulletin on Form ADV , the uniform registration filing divides into several distinct segments. Each part addresses different elements of an advisory firm's business practices and personnel. Part About What it contains Delivered to clients? Part 1 The advisory firm Check-the-box details on business operations, ownership structure, total clients, employee counts, business practices, corporate affiliations, and disciplinary events of the adviser or its employees Public on the IAPD website Part 2A The advisory firm Plain-English narrative brochure covering 18 standardized items, including advisory services, asset amounts, fee schedules, conflicts, risk descriptions, and disciplinary details Advisers must deliver the brochure to prospective and existing clients, and each year deliver a summary of material changes with a revised brochure or an offer to deliver one Part 2B Individual professionals Brochure supplement covering six items on individual background, including education, five-year business history, disciplinary history, and outside business activities Yes. Delivered for supervised individuals formulating advice or exercising discretion Part 3 The advisory firm Form CRS relationship summary covering services, fees, conflicts, required standard of conduct, disciplinary history, and key conversation starters Yes. Delivered to retail investors As summarized in the Investor.gov glossary entry on Form ADV , Part 1 provides structured business data, while Part 2 functions as the narrative disclosure document explaining practical terms. What to Look For in the Part 2A Brochure The Part 2A brochure contains 18 items presented in a standardized order so that you can evaluate multiple firms side by side. The SEC investor bulletin identifies the items below. Advisory business: The firm describes the types of advisory services it provides and discloses the total amount of client assets it manages. Reviewing this section helps you understand if the firm handles portfolio management, financial planning, or specialized strategies, which connects to the details in our guide to what is a registered investment advisor . Fees and compensation: The brochure outlines fee schedules, explains whether rates are negotiable, and specifies whether payments are billed directly to you or deducted from your account. It also lists additional expenses you might incur, such as brokerage commissions, custody charges, and underlying fund fees. You can use these details to assess total costs before signing an advisory contract. Performance-based fees and side-by-side management: An adviser that accepts performance-based fees, or supervises someone who does, must disclose it. If it also manages accounts without a performance fee, it must explain the resulting conflicts and how it addresses them. Methods of analysis, investment strategies, and risk of loss: The firm explains its research methods, core strategies, and the risks associated with its recommendations. Disciplinary information: The SEC bulletin explains that firms must disclose material legal or disciplinary events. Certain regulatory or legal actions within the last 10 years are presumed to be material. Code of ethics, participation in client transactions, and personal trading: The adviser must briefly describe its code of ethics, state that a copy is available on request, and disclose whether it or a related person invests in the same securities it recommends, with the conflicts involved. Brokerage practices: The adviser must describe how it selects broker-dealers and judges their compensation, and must disclose soft dollar practices. Every firm answers these 18 items in the exact same sequence. That fixed layout allows you to open two brochures from competing firms and compare identical sections without searching through different page structures. Reviewing Part 2B, Part 3, and Part 1 for Complete Background While Part 2A covers the entire firm, the Part 2B brochure supplement focuses on the individual professional handling your money. The SEC bulletin explains that an adviser must deliver this supplement for each supervised individual who formulates investment advice and maintains direct client contact, or who exercises discretionary trading authority over client assets. The Part 2B supplement covers six specific items. It outlines the individual's formal education, business background over the past five years, disciplinary information, and outside business activities. Part 3, also known as the relationship summary or Form CRS, provides a succinct comparison format. Per Investor.gov guidance on Form CRS , the relationship summary covers services offered, fees and costs, conflicts of interest, required standards of conduct, legal or disciplinary history, and key conversation starters. It serves as an accessible starting point before you dig into the comprehensive narrative of Part 2A. Part 1 remains available on the SEC IAPD portal for investors who want institutional data. It uses a check-the-box layout to record exact ownership structures, business practices, employee counts, corporate affiliations, and disciplinary events involving the firm or its staff. If a firm operates under several parent entities or affiliates, Part 1 lists those corporate connections. Check the Person and the Firm Check both the firm and the individual representative on IAPD. Check any broker on FINRA BrokerCheck , and read their Form CRS (Investor.gov: registered broker-dealers must provide one). See what a registered investment advisor is and how conflicts of interest work. Limits of Form ADV and When the Answer Changes The SEC bulletin describes Form ADV as the form investment advisers use to register. For a broker, check FINRA BrokerCheck and read their Form CRS . In our editorial judgment, a clean Form ADV filing does not show advice quality. Certain conditions will change how you read Form ADV or alter the conclusions you draw from the text: The adviser delivers a new annual summary of material changes: read it against the brochure you already have. A newly recorded legal or disciplinary event appears in Part 1 or Part 2B, requiring you to reconsider whether to keep the relationship under the guidelines in our breakdown of when to switch financial advisors . The brochure says fees are negotiable: your contract sets the fees you pay (Investor.gov), so compare the contract with the Part 2A fee schedule. How to Read Form ADV and Take Practical Action Open the Part 2A brochure and confirm the fee method matches what the adviser told you. Read the Part 2B supplement for the person who will handle your account. Bring any unclear item to the adviser as a written question before you sign. A clean filing does not show advice quality, so use it to ask better questions. Frequently asked questions Is Form ADV public? Yes, Form ADV is a public document. Form ADV filings for registered investment advisory firms and their representatives are public on the SEC Investment Adviser Public Disclosure database. How do I search Form ADV? You can search Form ADV by visiting the Investor.gov Check Out Your Investment Professional search tool, which directs you to the SEC Investment Adviser Public Disclosure portal. Enter the firm or individual advisor name to view their current filings. What is Form ADV Part 2A? Form ADV Part 2A is the narrative brochure that registered investment advisers must prepare. It contains 18 standardized items written in plain English, detailing services offered, fee schedules, conflicts of interest, investment strategies, and disciplinary information. What is Form ADV Part 3? Form ADV Part 3, also known as Form CRS, is the relationship summary document designed for retail investors. It provides concise information about the firm's services, fees and costs, conflicts of interest, standard of conduct, and disciplinary history. Is Form ADV annual? The SEC bulletin says advisers must deliver a summary of material changes to clients every year, along with a revised brochure or an offer to deliver one. What Is Investment Management? By Jonathan Velez , Personal Finance Writer & Editor · Reviewed against primary sources · Updated November 10, 2026 Investment management is choosing, monitoring, and adjusting investments for a specific financial goal. You can manage your own portfolio by making every trade yourself, or you can hire an adviser for ongoing oversight. Tools for this journey Investing → Retirement → Net worth → What Investment Management Is Investment management involves selecting securities, tracking their performance against defined objectives, and reallocating positions over time. Per guidance from Investor.gov on investing on your own , the first step in self-directed investing is creating a clear financial plan. That plan establishes how much capital you invest, how long you plan to invest, your specific goals, and your risk tolerance. When you invest on your own, you accept sole responsibility for every investment decision. Investor.gov notes that self-directed investors execute trades through online investing platforms, direct investing programs, or dividend reinvestment plans. In contrast, hiring an investment professional delegates ongoing portfolio oversight to an external manager. Investor.gov on investment advisers notes that an investment adviser is a firm or person paid to give advice about securities. Advisers generally provide ongoing recommendations about buying, selling, or holding securities. What an Investment Manager Does An investment manager provides ongoing portfolio oversight, performance reviews, and asset selection tailored to client goals. Under guidance published by Investor.gov on working with an investment professional , investment advisers are required to act in your best interest and cannot place their own interests ahead of yours. Advisers may also offer optional financial planning services alongside ongoing portfolio monitoring. In discretionary accounts, an adviser makes trades and delegated decisions. The scope of work provided by an adviser differs substantially from transaction-based brokerage services. As detailed on Investor.gov regarding the relationship summary (Form CRS) , brokers are generally transactional professionals paid commissions or markups per transaction. Investment advisers focus on managing your portfolio over time. Dual-registered firms operate under both models, so you should understand when they act as a broker and when as an adviser. What Assets Under Management Means for Account Fees According to the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) investor bulletin on Form ADV , an adviser must disclose the amount of client assets managed in Form ADV Part 2A. Investor.gov states that an adviser's fee is typically based on the value of all of the assets held in your account with the adviser. The Form CRS disclosure guidance explains that an asset-based fee can cost more than transaction-based fees. However, an asset-based fee aligns with continuous portfolio monitoring and delegated trading authority. Form ADV Part 2A requires firms to disclose whether fees are negotiable, how billing occurs, and whether custodial or fund expenses apply. Our flat-fee vs AUM financial advisers comparison covers the cost math for these pricing models. Decision Framework for Managing Investments or Hiring an Adviser Deciding between self-directed investing and hiring an investment adviser depends on required services, total costs, and potential conflicts. Investor.gov lists six things to check about an adviser: services, limits on services, total cost, how the adviser is paid, conflicts and legal or disciplinary history. Our judgment is that self-directed investing works best when you want complete control and have a clear financial plan. Your situation Do it yourself Hire an adviser What to check Portfolio planning Create your own financial plan Receive ongoing advice and optional planning Required services and account limits Trading authority Retain sole responsibility for trades Delegate discretionary trades Client contract terms and trading discretion Fee structure No ongoing advisory fee. You still pay other fees and costs related to services and investments (Investor.gov Form CRS page) Pay an ongoing asset-based fee on total account value Fee schedules and deduction methods Oversight requirements Monitor and rebalance your own holdings Rely on continuous professional oversight Form CRS relationship summary disclosures Professional history Check any broker you use on FINRA BrokerCheck Research background via public databases Form ADV Part 1 and Part 2 disciplinary history First decide whether you need ongoing monitoring. If you only require occasional guidance, paying an ongoing asset-based fee may be unnecessary. If you prefer continuous portfolio adjustments and delegated execution, hiring an adviser provides that service. See DIY vs hire and break-even to evaluate the tradeoff. Steps to Check an Investment Adviser Before Hiring Search both the person and the firm on the Investment Adviser Public Disclosure (IAPD) database through the Investor.gov professional search tool . Read the Form ADV Part 2A brochure fee items and the Form CRS relationship summary before you hire an adviser. The SEC makes these brochures and relationship summaries accessible on the Investment Adviser Public Disclosure (IAPD) database . To learn more about navigating these filings, review our guide on how to read Form ADV and our overview of what is a registered investment advisor . Situations Where Hiring an Adviser Does Not Fit Hiring an investment manager is not necessary for every investor. Hiring an adviser does not fit if you want self-direction and accept responsibility for every decision. Investor.gov notes that ways to invest on your own include online investing, direct investing, and dividend reinvestment plans. An asset-based fee is a fixed percentage of your balance, so it takes the same share of a small account as a large one. A flat subscription or minimum fee is the kind that can take a large share of a small balance: the SEC bulletin gives $3 a month on a $500 account, more than 7 percent a year. Your approach changes if you only need infrequent trade execution rather than ongoing portfolio supervision. A registered broker paid per transaction offers a different model that avoids ongoing asset-based management fees. Investor.gov notes that how financial professionals make money creates specific conflicts of interest, so you must always verify fee structures before entering into an advisory agreement. Our Takeaway on What Is Investment Management Investor.gov says investing on your own starts with a financial plan (how much, for how long, your goals and your tolerance for risk) and that you are responsible for your decisions. Hire an adviser if you want ongoing advice and monitoring, or someone to place trades for you, and accept an asset-based fee. Form CRS says that fee may cost more than a transaction-based fee. This is our reading of those sources, not an SEC recommendation. This decision changes if a flat or minimum fee would be a large share of your balance, or if your needs are met through single transactions executed by a broker. Write down your timeline and goals, read what a financial advisor does , and compare any adviser's Form CRS with the cost of investing on your own. Frequently asked questions What does assets under management mean? Assets under management (AUM) is the amount of client assets an adviser manages, which Form ADV Part 2A requires the adviser to disclose. What are assets under management fees? An assets under management fee is an advisory charge typically based on the value of all assets in your account. See flat-fee vs AUM advisors for the cost math. Is investment management the same as wealth management? Not exactly. Investment management is choosing and monitoring securities. A wealth manager generally adds tax and estate coordination for higher-net-worth clients, and neither title is legally regulated. See financial advisor vs wealth manager . Some advisors are fiduciaries, meaning they must put your interests first. Others, such as brokers, follow Regulation Best Interest, a separate SEC standard for broker-dealers. This guide covers the standards, fee models, the CFP credential, how to verify an advisor, and what to ask during your first call. Tools for this journey What is a registered investment advisor → Retirement → Investing → Net worth → What is a CTFA → Know Which Type of Financial Professional You're Talking To "Financial advisor" is a loose umbrella term, and the specific job title someone uses often says more about how they're paid and regulated than the word "advisor" itself does. An investment adviser registers with the SEC or a state regulator and owes you the fiduciary duty covered in Step 1 below, typically charging a fee tied to the assets under management. A broker-dealer representative can also call themselves a financial advisor, but is held to Regulation Best Interest, a separate SEC standard for broker-dealers, and is often paid a commission on what they sell. A few other titles are worth naming directly. A wealth advisor usually follows the same fiduciary model as an investment adviser, aimed at higher-net-worth clients with higher account minimums . A financial coach or financial counselor may offer many kinds of help, so ask what that specific person provides. A CPA who also advises on investments needs a separate license to do so legally, since the CPA credential itself covers tax and accounting work, not investment management. A robo-advisor replaces the human with an algorithm that builds and rebalances a portfolio automatically, usually at a much lower fee. Our robo-advisor vs. financial advisor breakdown covers when that trade-off makes sense. Two more titles show up mostly at larger firms or in specific situations. A portfolio or asset manager runs the investment decisions inside a fund or a large account. That person often never speaks directly to the end client, since a financial advisor is usually the relationship-facing role sitting between that manager and you. A financial therapist works on the emotional and behavioral side of money instead, like anxiety around spending or conflict with a partner over finances. That role typically isn't licensed to manage investments or give specific investment advice at all. The CFP credential from Step 3 below cuts across most of these titles, and so does the related but less common ChFC (Chartered Financial Consultant) designation. Each is a personal qualification a person earns, separate from which of the business models above they actually work under. A CFP or ChFC can work as a fee-only investment adviser, inside a wealth-management firm, or, less commonly, as a broker-dealer representative, and the fiduciary duty from Step 1 tracks that underlying role every time. Step 1: Understand fiduciary vs suitability The single most important test is the standard your advisor follows. A fiduciary is required by law to act in your best interest, disclose conflicts, and avoid self-dealing. The SEC applies this fiduciary duty to registered investment advisers under the Investment Advisers Act of 1940. Brokers historically only had to recommend something suitable, a weaker rule that allowed higher-fee products when a cheaper option would also fit. Regulation Best Interest now raises the broker standard, but it is still not the same as fiduciary duty. Ask any advisor in writing which standard covers each of your accounts, and read the firm's Form CRS. Our guide to what a fiduciary is explains which standard applies to advisers, brokers and CFP professionals. Step 2: Compare fee-only, commission, and hybrid How an advisor is paid shapes what they recommend. Fee-only advisors are paid only by you, either as a percentage of assets managed (often around 1% per year), a flat fee, or an hourly rate. This model reduces conflicts because their pay does not depend on which product you buy. Commission-based advisors earn from the products they sell you, like mutual funds, annuities, or insurance. Hybrid advisors can charge both. The SEC recommends comparing fees in actual dollars, not just percentages. A 1% fee on $500,000 is $5,000 a year, which needs to buy real value to be worth it. Step 3: Look for the CFP credential The CFP (Certified Financial Planner) is the most respected credential in personal financial planning. CFP professionals must complete college-level coursework, pass a rigorous exam, meet an experience requirement, and follow a code of ethics. CFP Board rules require them to act as fiduciaries when giving financial advice. Our guide to what a CFP is and what it takes to earn one lists the four certification requirements. Other credentials exist and vary widely in rigor. The SEC warns that professional designations do not all require the same difficulty, and some may indicate product limitations. A CFP with a fee-only fiduciary practice is a strong starting point for most families. If you're sizing up a fund manager rather than hiring a personal planner, see what a CFA charter actually means and how it differs from a CFP. Step 4: Verify the advisor before you hire Never hire an advisor without checking their record. The SEC provides two free tools you should always use. Investment Adviser Public Disclosure (IAPD) at adviserinfo.sec.gov shows the firm's Form ADV, services, fees, conflicts, and any disciplinary history. FINRA's BrokerCheck at brokercheck.finra.org covers brokers. The SEC also requires most advisors to give you Form CRS, the Customer Relationship Summary. It discloses services, fees, conflicts, and any disciplinary events in plain language. If someone will not send you a Form CRS or ADV, walk away. If you are replacing an advisor, see when to switch financial advisors before you move any accounts. Step 5: Questions to ask on the first call Bring the same short list to every advisor you interview. Ask: Which standard covers each of my accounts, in writing? How are you paid, exactly, and what will my total annual cost be in dollars? What credentials do you hold, and is one the CFP? Also ask: Who is your typical client, and do they look like me? How often will we meet, and who is my main contact? What happens to my accounts if you leave or retire? A good advisor answers each question directly. A vague or evasive answer is your signal to keep looking. For the full interview script, see our questions to ask a financial advisor . Frequently asked questions How do I choose a financial advisor? Choose a financial advisor by starting with the fiduciary standard, then the fee model, then credentials. A fee-only fiduciary who holds the CFP credential is a strong starting point. Always verify their record on SEC IAPD or FINRA BrokerCheck before you sign anything. What is a fiduciary financial advisor? A fiduciary financial advisor is legally required to act in your best interest. The SEC applies this fiduciary duty to registered investment advisers under the Investment Advisers Act of 1940. Brokers historically followed a weaker 'suitability' standard, though Regulation Best Interest now raises that bar. What is the difference between fee-only and commission? A fee-only advisor is paid only by you, through a percentage of assets, a flat fee, or an hourly rate. A commission-based advisor is paid by the companies whose products they sell. Fee-only reduces conflicts because the advisor's pay does not depend on which product you buy. What does CFP mean? CFP stands for Certified Financial Planner, the leading credential in personal financial planning. CFP professionals must complete college-level coursework, pass an exam, meet an experience requirement, and follow a code of ethics. CFP Board rules require them to act as fiduciaries when giving financial advice. How do I verify a financial advisor? Verify an advisor using the SEC's Investment Adviser Public Disclosure (IAPD) at adviserinfo.sec.gov and FINRA's BrokerCheck at brokercheck.finra.org. Both are free and show the advisor's firm, services, fees, and any disciplinary history. Also request Form CRS and Form ADV before hiring. How much does a financial advisor cost? Costs vary by model. A fee-only advisor may charge about 1% of assets managed per year, a flat annual fee of a few thousand dollars, or an hourly rate. On $500,000, a 1% fee is $5,000 a year, so compare fees in actual dollars, not just percentages. Where can I find a financial advisor? Start with SEC Investment Adviser Public Disclosure (IAPD) at adviserinfo.sec.gov or FINRA BrokerCheck at brokercheck.finra.org, which let you search for advisors directly by name or firm instead of relying on an ad. The CFP Board also maintains a directory of CFP professionals. Wherever you find candidates, run them through the same verification steps before you hire anyone. What's the difference between a financial advisor and a wealth advisor? Little in regulation, since a wealth advisor usually follows the same fiduciary standard as an investment adviser. The real difference is who they serve: a wealth advisor typically targets higher-net-worth clients and sets a higher account minimum, often $500,000 or more, while a general financial advisor works with a broader range of account sizes. Is a financial coach the same as a financial advisor? Not necessarily. Titles differ, so ask what that specific person provides and verify any registration or designation they claim. A financial advisor who manages a portfolio needs to be registered as an investment adviser or a broker-dealer representative, a different regulatory category entirely.
